The Gospel Transforms Us to Serve, Stand Firm, and Stick Together

Paul answers the rumour that he abandoned the Thessalonians — and turns the defence into a lesson on what the gospel keeps doing after it saves you: it makes you serve others, it holds you standing firm under persecution, and it will not let you go it alone.

Andy Robbins
44 min
Captured live
with Ahtend

The heart of a father

Back when I was a teenager I found myself sweeping out the annex of our caravan while we were on a family holiday up the coast. I'd like to say I was sweeping because I wanted to. I suspect I was told a million times, and then I started doing it. It didn't take long before my dad took the broom off me and started giving me lessons on how to sweep. I didn't realise there was a certain way to use a broom. Apparently there is.

SCENE
A father, a broom, and a lesson

As a teenager Andy was sweeping out the annex of the family caravan on a holiday up the coast when his dad took the broom off him and he found himself in a lesson. His father was not flexing about how knowledgeable and skilful he was with a broom — he was being a dad, shepherding his son, teaching him, hoping he might learn and grow to know how to use a broom well.

In fairness to my dear father, he wasn't flexing about how knowledgeable and skilful he is with a broom. My dad was being a dad. He could see I was doing something that wasn't so great, and there's this part of a dad that goes: I want to help. I want to teach. I want my son to become an adult who knows how to use a broom properly. It wasn't him going, hey, back in my day. It was a father shepherding his son, hoping he might learn.

SLIDE
Thessalonians: Living in Light of His Return

Week three of the series. Paul had preached the gospel in Thessalonica two years earlier and then fled persecution; in his absence the rumours started.

Paul had visited Thessalonica a couple of years earlier. He preached the gospel to them, and then all of a sudden he had to get out of there, because he was facing persecution. Since he's been gone, there had been gossip taking place. Rumours. He doesn't care about you. He's moved on. When Paul came, it was for selfish reasons and selfish ambition.

So as he writes to this bunch of young Christians, working out what it looks like to follow Jesus for the first time, he has to address those rumours — because rightfully, they're starting to wonder whether they're true. Has Paul really just moved on and forgotten about us? Did he really come for selfish motives?

But here's the thing we need to pay attention to. As he addresses them, we can read it like Paul is just flexing about how good he is. That's not what Paul's doing. He's seeking to teach, to show, like the heart of a father towards his child. He wants these young people not just to understand something, but to know it.

Point 1

Serve Others

Paul writes like a man who has been orphaned — an intense longing, every effort made to get back, and Satan blocking the way. He calls this church his hope, his joy, his crown.

Doesn't Paul's letter to this church just ooze with deep love and affection for these people? Look at the language he uses. He is not nonchalant about a group of Christians he saw two years ago and is now far away from. Do you get the sense that Paul has forgotten about them? That he's moved on, that he doesn't care? Not at all.

He felt orphaned when they were separated. He had an intense longing to be with them again, and made every effort to get there. That is a deep kind of love, isn't it? In fact it goes further. He considers these people a crown — a crown that he, Timothy and Silas would boast in when the Lord Jesus returns.

Boy, oh boy, we like to boast, don't we? Anybody on Facebook? What do we love to do? How good am I. Here's my awesome holiday. Here's my awesome cereal that I just prepared. Here are my high school grades, here's my fifteen degrees, here's my new job. We're good at boasting. But are we boasting the wrong things?

QUESTION
If Jesus came back right now

"If Jesus came back right now, what do you want to show him? What do you want to show him more than anything else?" Paul's answer is the people God brought to life through his ministry.

So what is Paul boasting in? Not his achievements. Not his degrees, not his income, not his dress sense, not his personality or his smile. It's the very people God brought to life through his ministry. It's the church.

And this wasn't a selfish boast. This wasn't Paul going, look how good I am, Jesus, look at all the people I saved. Paul knows. You see it in the first chapter of this book: Paul saves no one. It's the power of the gospel, coming in deep conviction with the Holy Spirit, that saves people. His boast isn't look what I've done. It's God, look how good you are.

SLIDE
Serve Others — 2:17-20

Hand-annotated on the day: "you?" circled, and "you are our glory and joy" underlined.

"Our greatest boast is not anything we have or our achievements. Our greatest boast is Christ. Our greatest boast is his achievements."

Andy Robbins

On the day that Jesus returns, the only things worth boasting in are things that last. The size of your house won't really matter much to God, the King of the universe. How far you got in your career — those things won't last.

You may not be an apostle. You're not, and neither am I. We weren't given the very specific task of taking the good news of Jesus to the Gentile world. But I suspect our hope, joy and crown should be no different.

My greatest boast right now is that Jesus Christ would take me from eternal death to eternal life. And what can I add to that boast? Only that God would use this frail, sinful man to help take that gospel to others, in the hope that they too might go from death to life. That is not just my greatest boast. That will be my only boast on the day I stand before the Lord Jesus Christ.

The gospel transforms us to see that serving others is the greatest hope, joy and crown we could give our lives to. For that is what Christ Jesus himself did. He came to serve and not be served. And the best way that you and I can serve others is to show them Jesus Christ.

Point 2

Stand Firm

Unable to return himself, Paul sends Timothy — his apprentice — to strengthen them. And the reason matters: Paul was afraid, "maybe even a little anxious… because Paul was a human being."

As we enter chapter 3, we read that even though Paul wasn't able to return to this young church himself, he sends his apprentice, Timothy — to strengthen and encourage them in their faith, and to report back on how they're going.

Because Paul was actually afraid. Maybe even a little anxious. And that's important for us to know, because Paul was a human being. He knew they were facing trials and persecution. He knew that Satan was out to get them, and he had a fear that this hostility was impacting their faith. Causing them to step back a little. To doubt, to question, or even to wonder.

Then Timothy returns. And I reckon — this is a guess, so don't hold on to it too tightly — Paul was a little bit surprised by what came back. He was fearful they were stumbling or wandering. Timothy comes back, and it's good news. Despite all that they are facing, this young church is holding.

"To hear and to know that this young church, this young group of Christians, despite all that they are facing, are standing firm."

Andy Robbins

It's as if Paul was carrying a weight, a burden, a deep concern that the hardship was hurting a church he loved, and now his distress is replaced with encouragement.

WORK
1 & 2 Thessalonians For You

Duncan's book-length walk through the letter Andy is preaching from, published by The Good Book Company in 2022. It covers the same ground at length — including what it takes to stand firm when those challenges come.

PERSON
Ligon Duncan

Chancellor of Reformed Theological Seminary, and for seventeen years the senior minister of First Presbyterian Church in Jackson, Mississippi. Andy leans on him twice in this talk — once on suffering, once on community.

But the language is important here. Paul makes it clear that they're not standing firm in their own strength, or effort, or determination. They're standing firm in the Lord. Their strength to endure the waves of opposition and hardship comes from belonging to and being in Jesus.

INSIGHT
Not their strength — their location

They are not standing firm by determination. They are standing firm in the Lord, and Andy names that the secret source.

They might be in Thessalonica, but more importantly — as we saw a fortnight ago — they are in Christ. In his power. In his protection, his provision, his purpose, his peace. They're weathering the storms coming at them, and not because they're tough people, and not because they've been Christians for decades. Ligon Duncan has a line about suffering that I keep coming back to, and it's worth having in mind for what Paul says next.

And Paul isn't surprised that they're facing hardship. He's concerned about what that hardship is doing to their faith, but he is not surprised that persecution has come. In fact it's the opposite: he warned them again and again that they would have it too.

TAKEAWAY
What standing firm actually looks like

"Everything that I'm about to tell you will not surprise you." Be in the Word, regularly and daily. Be in Christian community — because the greater danger is not water but Satan.

Paul says in verse 3 that this is what we are destined for, and he had told them so while he was still with them — not to frighten them, but so that when hardship came they would recognise it for what it was, rather than conclude that God had abandoned them. Ligon Duncan puts it more bluntly than I would dare to.

Suffering — we are destined for it. If you are a Christian, you will suffer. The Christian life is not just prancing along, bouncing on a rainbow until you get to heaven. Suffering and affliction and trials should not be a surprise for Christians.

Ligon Duncan1

The only thing strong enough to help you and I stand firm when those challenges come — whether it's the result of living in a sinful world, or of Satan prowling out to kill and destroy — is Jesus. It's not you. It's not a spouse. It's not your family, or your friends, or your income, or your insurance plans. Only Jesus is bigger than sin, and only Jesus is bigger and stronger than Satan himself.

SCENE
The drive to swimming lessons

Andy's son hates swimming lessons and cannot see the point, and the drive there each week is not a fun one. "There's going to be a time where you've got a license and a car and you're going to want to go to the beach with your friend… you're not going to want daddy there with you holding you in the waves." The discipline of going every week is for his freedom — and for the danger the water really poses. Christians face a greater danger than water: not just sin, but Satan.

I have a son who really hates swimming lessons at the moment. Really, really doesn't like swimming lessons. And every week I pick him up from school to go to said swimming lesson. Boy, oh boy, it's a fun drive to swimming. He doesn't want to go. He does not see the point.

And I say to him: buddy, the water is dangerous, really dangerous. The discipline of going to swimming lessons week in and week out is preparing you for that danger. It's giving you the skills and the ability to weather it. Without it, you're in big trouble.

Now, as Christians, we have a greater danger than water. And it's not just sin. It's Satan. So how do we weather that storm? We stand firm in Christ. Which raises the obvious question, and it's the one I want to answer before we move on: what does standing firm in Christ actually look like?

Point 3

Stick Together

Paul's prayer for a persecuted church is not the prayer you would expect — and what he asks for binds love and holiness together so tightly that neither can be pursued on its own.

As Paul reflects on this encouraging report that Timothy brings back, he cannot help but stop and pray for a church he loves deeply.

Paul could have prayed anything here. Anything. He doesn't pray that the opposition would stop, or that their circumstances would change. I'm sure he wants that. That's not what he prays, at least not in this letter to them.

He prays that God would make their love for each other increase and overflow, and that God would strengthen their hearts, in the hope that they'd be found holy and blameless when Jesus comes back. What's interesting here is that Paul intertwines growing in godliness with loving one another. You see that? He prays their love would increase and overflow, and the very next thing is that they would grow in godliness. He intertwines the two. It's as if Paul is saying: you need each other. We've got to stick together as a church.

Two chapters of longing and defence: Paul explains why he has not come back, sends Timothy in his place, and closes by praying for the church he cannot reach.

1 Thessalonians 2:17 – 3:13

"Growing in godliness isn't a solo sport."

Andy Robbins

For those who don't know me, I'm the middle child — so if you're trying to work out what's wrong with that guy, middle children unite. I've got an older sister and a younger brother, but most of my childhood, if I'm honest, I felt like an only child, because neither of my siblings liked sport. Any sport. Neither of them.

SCENE
Nobody to play with

Andy wanted to get better at soccer, so he spent his afternoons kicking a ball at his dad's garage door — until the dents got him in trouble. So he switched to the brick wall in the backyard, the one above his mum's garden bed. "Well, guess what? The broken pots got him in trouble too. Trying to get better at a team sport when nobody at home would play it proved not just difficult but impossible: a brick wall doesn't respond as much as another person does.

Paul prays that their love would increase and overflow — and Andy presses the implication. "My love for you can't increase and overflow if I don't know you. So if we are going to stick together, if we're going to love one another, then we must know one another. You cannot love what you do not know."

Andy Robbins

So I'd get home from school wanting nothing more than to kick a ball or play cricket, and I found myself most afternoons kicking a soccer ball into my dad's garage door — until he got home from work and I got in trouble for the dents I'd put in it. So then I started kicking the ball up against a brick wall in the backyard, which was just above my mum's garden bed. Well, guess what: I've got a great aim. So then I broke mum's pots, and I got in trouble for that too.

We live in a very individualised culture, and it has crept into the church. I suspect you will know people who say they believe in Jesus, they're a Christian, but they have no desire and no movement in their life to connect with other Christians. It's my faith, I do it my way. It's not in the Bible. Christians need each other. You cannot follow Jesus alone.

Which is where I want to bring Duncan back in, on the question of where the virtues of the Christian life actually get grown.

The virtues of the Christian life cannot be cultivated in isolation from one another. We need to be in community and we need to be in accountability in order to cultivate the virtues of the Christian life.

Ligon Duncan · "Living in Light of Jesus' Return: A Good Report of Faith", sermon on 1 Thessalonians 3:6–13, First Presbyterian Church, Jackson, 17 June 2012

What I'm asking for is more costly than turning up. Being in community is not an optional extra for a Christian. It is the outworking of the gospel in your life. We need to be in close community with people who are different to us — people who will test and stretch our patience, generosity, conviction and care, and who will love us enough to gently but courageously call out sin and ungodly behaviour. We need models of what it looks like to be a godly parent or a godly spouse. We need single people who show us the sufficiency of Jesus Christ above all else. We need to see saints face death with a courageous faith.

Sticking together means more than just showing up on a Sunday. It means more than just sitting with and talking to the same few people every time we come. Sticking together is loving one another. And the prayer sets the bar higher than politeness: a love that will increase and overflow is not something you can do at arm's length. To get anywhere near it, we have to know one another.

Sticking together also looks like serving one another. If we're coming simply to be entertained, to receive a product and go home, that is not the Christian heart. That's not the work of the gospel. It looks like getting involved in the mess of one another's lives. It looks like welcoming people into our lives and our homes.

The gospel is at work

What a hope we have as we leave here this morning — to go back to our homes and families, our workplaces and communities this week, and to know that the gospel is at work. The gospel that saved us, the one that came in great power and deep conviction through the work of the Holy Spirit, continues to work. To transform us. To help us serve others and pour ourselves out for the sake of the gospel. To help us remember that we can stand firm against sin and against Satan himself, because we're in Christ.

"Not Paul is great, but the gospel is great." The rumours about him are not true, Andy says, because the gospel that saved Paul is still at work in Paul — and it keeps working in us long after we are saved.

Andy Robbins

And what a call we have to answer: to stick together. Not just to show up and go home, but to get to know, to serve, to be part of the people that God has welcomed you into — that you and I might grow in godliness as we love one another, all the more until Jesus returns.

In closing

Keep going

"Brothers and sisters, the gospel that saved you is at work within you. And he who began that good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day that Christ returns. That's our hope. Keep going. Keep trusting Christ."
